case.title: Hollinwick's council tenants are behind on the rent
case.question: Should the council chase unpaid rent harder, or help tenants clear their debts first?
case.story: Hollinwick council owns 6,200 homes, and 2,670 of its tenants now owe rent, which is 43 per cent. The average debt is about £675 a household, and the council is owed £1.8 million in all. The housing budget is fixed at £4.1 million for the year, and the council can spend £350,000 more only by cutting repairs. Councillors can send tougher letters and start evictions sooner, or pay for debt advisers and payment plans that take longer to bring money back. Some tenants are in work but squeezed. Others are ill, or waiting on benefits.

in_the_news.headline: Council rent arrears surge 57% as tenant debts mount
in_the_news.why: A study of 108 councils found 43% of council homes have unpaid rent, so Hollinwick's choice is the one many councils face.

facts.text: 43% of council homes in the study had unpaid rent in 2026, up from 37% in 2025.
The average debt per household in arrears was £674.62.
The study used freedom of information answers from 108 councils.

sources.title: Council rent arrears surge 57% as tenant debts mount

made_by.note: Round 2: the citizens' tests were too easy (answer A passed all five), so t1 and t2 were made more exact. No mark was edited.

tests.text: Says how much of the £1.8 million comes back in 12 months, and how many staff it takes and what they cost a year.
Says how many days a tenant with a late benefit is left alone, and who chases the benefit office.
Gives a date by which tenants in arrears are first contacted by a named person, not a form letter.
Never starts eviction over arrears under £1,500, and never over any debt while a payment plan is being kept.
Pays for it without cutting the £4.1 million repairs and housing budget or raising rents.

voices.who: a woman in her 30s who cannot work through illness, a council tenant
voices.text: When my payment was late I was frightened of the letters. I want a person who rings me, not another threat.

voices.who: a man in his 50s in work, a council tenant
voices.text: I pay on time and it costs me. I want the rent chased, but nobody should lose their home over a few hundred quid.

voices.who: a woman in her 80s, a council tenant
voices.text: I have lived here all my life. If the repairs stop because of other people's debts, that is not fair on me.

voices.who: a retired man in his 80s who owns his home
voices.text: The council is spending my council tax on this. Tell me how much comes back and when.

bench.angle: Help first: advisers and payment plans before letters
bench.title: Help first: a named adviser rings every tenant in arrears
bench.answer:
What changes: By 31 January, a named adviser phones each of the 2,670 tenants in arrears. No form letter comes first. Advisers set up payment plans.

Benefit delays: if a tenant is behind only because a payment is late, nothing is chased. They ring their named adviser, who chases the benefit office.

Limits: no eviction over arrears under £1,500, or while a plan is kept.

Who pays: the advisers are paid from the existing £4.1 million, using money now spent on letters and court steps. Repairs and rents stay as they are.

Target: £900,000 of the £1.8 million back within 12 months, collected by the adviser team. Monthly reports show plans kept, rent paid and repairs spend.

bench.angle: Firm but fair: staged letters, eviction as last step
bench.title: Firm but fair: a named officer first, staged letters, eviction last
bench.answer:
Step 1: within 10 working days of falling behind, a named rent officer rings the tenant. Step 2: a payment plan. Step 3: a firm letter if the plan is ignored. Step 4: a final warning. Eviction is only for debts over £1,500, and never while a plan is kept. A tenant waiting on a late benefit gets time, and rings their rent officer.

Rent officers and advisers are paid from the existing £4.1 million, with no repairs cut and no rent rise. We aim to get back £900,000 of the £1.8 million in 12 months. We'd know it worked if arrears fall by that much and few cases reach court.

bench.angle: Write off small debts, chase large ones hard
bench.title: Forgive the small debts, chase the big ones hard
bench.answer: Write off debts under £250 for tenants who are ill or waiting on benefits. Chase larger debts with a named housing officer who rings each tenant within 14 days of the council's vote. Tenants held up by a late benefit pay nothing extra while it is fixed, and they ring their officer. No eviction under £1,500, or while a plan is kept. Pay from the £4.1 million housing budget, with no repair cuts and no rent rise. We do not yet know how much of the £1.8 million is small debts. Officers count them in 30 days and publish a figure for what comes back in 12 months. Success: arrears fall each quarter.

gate.verdict: All three keep both limits (t4, t5), but none gives staff numbers or cost (t1) or the days and who chases the benefit office (t2). Only A names a date for first contact (t3). C is weakest, with no recovery figure at all.

jury.question: If a tenant ignores their adviser for six months, what should the council do?
options: Keep trying to help them, however long it takes
Allow court action after six months, for debts over £1,500 only
Visit them at home first, then allow court action after six months
jury.ruling: Allow court action after six months, for debts over £1,500 only, won 5 votes to 4 and 3.

reasons.text: I'd not like to see a neighbour put out. Keep knocking on the door.
Those who pay shouldn't carry those who won't. Six months is long enough.
I pay on time. Someone should visit first, so we know who can't and who won't.

minister.text: A six-month trial of answer A: a named adviser rings every tenant in arrears, with no eviction under £1,500 or while a plan is kept. It tests 3 of 5 tests passed, 2 unclear, 0 failed.
minister.statement: Bea Hartwell: I won't sign all of this yet. Answer A kept both red lines and gave a date, 31 January, for a named person to ring every tenant. But it didn't say how many advisers it needs, what they cost, or how many days a late benefit is left alone. The citizens' jury said court action after six months, for debts over £1,500 only, and the trial will use that. We'll count the keys kept, not the letters sent.
